reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / standard rheumatology references
clinicalPearls: A group of monogenic autoinflammatory disorders unified by constitutive overproduction of type I interferon
Aicardi-Goutieres syndrome is a prototypic form presenting with an early encephalopathy, intracranial calcifications, white matter disease, and CSF lymphocytosis mimicking congenital infection
STING-associated vasculopathy with onset in infancy (SAVI) features severe cutaneous vasculopathy with acral necrosis, interstitial lung disease, and systemic inflammation

The CANDLE syndrome (chronic atypical neutrophilic dermatosis with lipodystrophy and elevated temperature), caused by proteasome-related mutations, presents with recurrent fever, annular skin lesions, and progressive lipodystrophy
Skin, brain, and lung are commonly targeted, and clinical overlap with congenital infection or systemic lupus erythematosus is frequent
A raised interferon signature (upregulated interferon-stimulated gene expression in blood) supports the diagnosis, confirmed by identifying the causative gene
Because interferon rather than IL-1 drives disease, standard IL-1 blockade is often ineffective, whereas JAK inhibitors that dampen interferon signalling are a rational therapy
These disorders illustrate the concept that dysregulated innate antiviral signalling can produce sterile, self-directed inflammation
reference.pathophysiology: Type I interferonopathies result from genetic defects that cause inappropriate sensing of self nucleic acids or impaired regulation of the interferon pathway, leading to chronic overproduction of type I interferon. Depending on the gene involved (for example nucleic acid metabolism enzymes in Aicardi-Goutieres syndrome, STING gain-of-function in SAVI, or proteasome dysfunction in CANDLE), sustained interferon signalling drives tissue inflammation, vasculopathy, and organ damage in the absence of infection.
additionalDifferentials: Systemic lupus erythematosus and other connective tissue diseases
additionalInvestigations: Interferon signature / interferon-stimulated gene expression assay
Targeted genetic or gene-panel testing for causative mutations
Neuroimaging showing intracranial calcification and white matter change in relevant forms
High-resolution chest imaging for interstitial lung disease (e.g. in SAVI)
Autoantibody testing to help distinguish from lupus
redFlags: Progressive neurological deterioration and developmental regression
Digital or acral necrosis and severe vasculopathy
Progressive interstitial lung disease with respiratory failure
Misdiagnosis as congenital infection leading to inappropriate or delayed treatment
reference.prognosis: Outcomes vary widely by subtype and severity; several forms cause significant neurological disability, disfiguring vasculopathy, or progressive lung disease with early mortality, though interferon-directed therapies such as JAK inhibition can improve inflammation and, in some patients, halt progression.
pitfalls: Mistaking the presentation for congenital infection or systemic lupus erythematosus
Expecting IL-1 blockade to work when the driver is type I interferon
Failing to obtain an interferon signature or genetic testing in unexplained early-onset multisystem inflammation
Overlooking progressive lipodystrophy or lung disease as part of the syndrome
management: Block interferon signalling with JAK inhibitors (such as baricitinib or ruxolitinib) as targeted disease-modifying therapy
Use corticosteroids and other immunosuppression to control acute inflammation while establishing targeted treatment

Provide organ-directed supportive care: management of interstitial lung disease, wound care for acral necrosis and cutaneous vasculopathy, and neurodevelopmental and anticonvulsant support in Aicardi-Goutieres syndrome
Monitor the interferon signature and affected organs (neurological, pulmonary and cutaneous) to gauge response and progression
Manage vascular and thrombotic complications and treat inflammatory flares promptly
Confirm the causative gene and provide genetic counselling and family screening for these monogenic disorders
Coordinate care across rheumatology, immunology, neurology and respiratory medicine
